To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we found that the salivary biomarker, calprotectin (S100A9) is significantly higher in pulmonary tuberculosis patients than healthy controls, and the levels of calprotectin are significantly reduced in pulmonary tuberculosis patients after 2 months of treatment, which suggests the potential for this biomarker to be used as a diagnostic marker for pulmonary tuberculosis, and as a biomarker to monitor the treatment response of pulmonary tuberculosis.

the salivary biomarkers of pulmonary tuberculosis are: (i) host biomarkers that are not secreted in saliva in the absence of tuberculosis disease, (ii) biomarkers that can be detected in the saliva of patients with active tuberculosis disease and (iii) biomarkers that decrease in saliva after the initiation of tuberculosis treatment and can therefore serve as a marker of the response to therapy.
we found that the levels of 2 host biomarkers (IL-6 and IL-8) in saliva samples were associated with the risk of developing pulmonary tuberculosis and with the treatment response.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of host biomarkers in the saliva of tuberculosis (TB) patients for the diagnosis of TB disease and monitoring of response to treatment.

the development and validation of host biomarker-based diagnostic tests and the development of a new approach to the monitoring of the response of tuberculosis patients to anti-tuberculosis treatment.
the development of host biomarkers for the diagnosis of tuberculosis disease and monitoring the response to tuberculosis treatments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there are no biomarkers for TB that can be recommended for use in clinical practice, but there is a strong potential for biomarkers to be useful for the diagnosis and treatment monitoring of TB in the future, particularly in the context of the development of new TB drugs.
the evidence is insufficient to support a recommendation for or against using saliva biomarkers to diagnose pulmonary tuberculosis or to monitor the response to tuberculosis therapy.
saliva biomarkers for tuberculosis disease diagnosis and monitoring of treatment response are promising but still need to be validated in larger and more diverse patient cohorts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified a panel of 12 host biomarkers that show promise for diagnosis of pulmonary TB.
host biomarkers in saliva show great promise as a tool for the diagnosis of active pulmonary tuberculosis disease and for monitoring of the treatment response.
host biomarkers detected in human saliva can be used for the diagnosis of tuberculosis disease and monitoring the response to tuberculosis therapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the host biomarkers detected in whole saliva are promising markers for the diagnosis and monitoring of pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) disease.
we have identified a set of biomarkers that can be used for diagnosis and treatment monitoring of tuberculosis.
the host biomarkers we have identified are promising as markers for the detection of tuberculosis and the monitoring of the response of tuberculosis to treatment.
